title: Contraction
hook: Luria taught that God withdrew to make room for a world

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Zohar dressed the Torah in its stories, with a body and a soul underneath. Your line was look beneath the garment. Whose inside did you catch sight of? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-three.

Before anyone new can sit at a crowded table, somebody has to scoot over. A small thing. A chair pulled back, a bag moved, an elbow tucked in. The table doesn't grow. The people already at it draw in a little. In the town of Safed, a teacher named Isaac Luria, whom his students called the Ari, asked something like it about everything there is. If God is without end and fills all things, where was there room for a world? His answer begins with a drawing in. Today's word.
screen: `SOMEBODY HAS TO SCOOT OVER.` → `GOD FILLS ALL THINGS.` → `WHERE IS THERE ROOM?`

segments.voice: Tzimtzum. The Hebrew means a contraction, a narrowing, a drawing in. Luria's teaching reaches us through his student Chaim Vital, in a work called Etz Chaim, the Tree of Life. Turn it four ways. First, the problem. Before anything was made, Vital writes, the light of the Infinite, the Ein Sof we met not long ago, filled everything. There was no empty space at all. Nowhere for a world to be. Second, the withdrawing. So the Infinite drew itself in, away from a center, and left an open space: a place where something other than God could exist. In this picture, creation starts with a stepping back. Third, the thin line. Into that open space, Vital writes, came a single line of light, reaching in from the Infinite. The space is never cut off. Whatever lives there is held by that thread. Fourth, the argument. Later teachers disagreed about how to read this. Some took the withdrawal at its word. Others, Hasidic teachers among them, said God never truly leaves any place, and the contraction is a hiding, so the world can have a place of its own. Both readings keep a God who makes space rather than taking it all. And some readers hear a human echo in it. A parent who goes quiet so a child can try. A teacher who leaves a question open. A friend who lets you finish your own sentence. Look back at this week: giving and holding back, harmony, the presence that dwells among us, companions on the road, the garment and the soul. Today it narrows to one small, deliberate space.
screen: `NO ROOM FOR A WORLD.` · `THE INFINITE DRAWS IN.` · `A SINGLE LINE OF LIGHT.` · `READ AS LEAVING, OR AS HIDING.` · then, large: `MAKE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make room for someone. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one person who could use a little more space from you. Maybe you talk over them, or fix things before they've asked, or fill every silence. Picture the next time you're together. See yourself leaving a pause. Not walking away, just drawing in a little, so there's room. Notice what might grow in that space: their words, their idea, their own way of doing it. Rest there, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Tzimtzum. Contraction: in Luria's teaching, the Infinite drawing in to leave room for a world. Today's word.
Your line: make room. Today, in one conversation, let the other person finish, and leave one more breath of quiet before you answer. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Tzimtzum is studied in Lurianic Kabbalah through Chaim Vital's Etz Chaim and its commentaries, and Hasidic teachers return to it often, especially in discussions of how God can be everywhere and a world can still exist.

myth: in Luria's picture, creation begins by pushing outward
it begins with a drawing in, which leaves an open space.
Luria's teaching reaches us through his student Chaim Vital
Vital set it down in Etz Chaim, the Tree of Life.
every teacher reads the contraction literally
later teachers disagreed; some Hasidic teachers read it as a hiding, not a leaving.

fork.setup: you are the Infinite, and you fill everything. there's no room for a world. what does Luria's teaching say happens?
options: the Infinite draws in and leaves an open space.
the world is made somewhere outside God.
fork.reveal: creation starts with a withdrawing: the Infinite draws in, and a single line of light reaches into the space left open.

original.note: Hebrew: contraction, narrowing, a drawing in.

trapdoor: what it means: in Luria's teaching, the Infinite draws in to leave an open space where a world can be.
what a scholar hears: Etz Chaim's opening on the empty space and the single line of light, and the later debate over whether tzimtzum is literal or a concealment.
recall: a city on the Sea of Galilee

notes: Editor pass: 'the Ein Sof we met earlier this week' changed to 'not long ago' (Ein Sof was day 1174, more than a week back); hook's 'a version of that question' (no question had been asked) smoothed to 'something like it'.

Etz Chaim's opening paraphrased: before creation the Infinite light filled all; it contracted away from a center, leaving an empty space, into which a single line (kav) of light was drawn. Please confirm the reference and paraphrase.

The disagreement over whether tzimtzum is literal is stated generally ('later teachers disagreed'); Tanya, Sha'ar ha-Yichud ve-ha-Emunah ch. 7 is cited for the Hasidic (Chabad) reading as concealment. Please confirm the citation and that the framing ranks no school.
'In the town of Safed' and 'whom his students called the Ari' are stated without dates under the claims rule; please confirm.

Week-end look-back names days 1177–1182 by theme (Chesed and Gevurah, Tiferet, Netzach/Hod/Yesod are folded into 'giving and holding back, harmony'); confirm it reads well with those scripts once written.
The human echo (parent, teacher, friend) is framed as 'some readers hear', not as a teaching of Luria.
